title: Referral and reactivation as a repeatable follow-up system
audience: Owners and lead practitioners who want a dependable stream of referrals and returning clients
learningOutcomes: Map each step of the enquiry-to-client process and set a time target for each
Write a referral request that is specific and timed to a client milestone
Plan a reactivation message for former clients that respects consent and opt-outs

instruction.heading: Fix the process before adding leads
instruction.body: Many businesses think they lack enquiries when the real problem is slow or uneven handling after an enquiry arrives. Write each step from the first reply through to the initial visit: reply, call or consultation, offer, booking and follow-up. Set a time target for each step. A prospect who waits two days for a reply may already have chosen someone else. Follow-up wins many enquiries, so keep a dated record of each follow-up.

instruction.heading: Ask for referrals at the right moment
instruction.body: The strongest moment for a request is after a client reaches a milestone they value, or when they say they are satisfied. Make the request specific: say what kind of person you help, and offer an easy route for passing on your details, such as a card or a booking link. Thank each person who refers and tell them what happened. Track the source of every referral so you know which requests work.

instruction.heading: Reactivate former clients with an honest check-in
instruction.body: Former clients often respond to a short message that asks about their goals and offers a no-pressure next step. Keep the tone plain. Where a message is sent electronically, the Spam Act applies, so confirm consent before sending. Remove anyone who opts out at once. A reactivation list is a list of people who may welcome contact, not a list to be emailed in bulk.

procedure: Write the enquiry process from first reply through to the initial visit and time each step.
Set a same-day target for first reply and track whether it is met for one month.
Choose a referral moment and a specific request for each client type.
Build a reactivation list with the consent status recorded for each person.
Log each referral and each reactivation reply, and review monthly.

workedExamples.situation: A hypothetical trainer finds enquiries wait about two days for a first reply, and six former clients have not trained for four months.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the trainer do first, and what should the reactivation message include?
workedExamples.reasoning: The reply delay is a process step with a measurable target, so set a same-day reply target first. For the reactivation list, check the consent basis for each person before any electronic message. A plain check-in that asks about goals and offers an easy next step, with a clear opt-out, is appropriate.

equipmentAndPpe: Referral card or link carrying no personal data

commonErrors.error: Asking for referrals before the client has seen results
commonErrors.prevention: Wait for a milestone or a clear expression of satisfaction.

commonErrors.error: Sending reactivation messages to a bought or scraped list
commonErrors.prevention: Use only addresses with a recorded consent basis, and check the Spam Act rules first.

commonErrors.error: Not tracking which referral requests work
commonErrors.prevention: Record the source of every enquiry and every referral.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Electronic reactivation messages are commercial electronic messages under the Spam Act 2003: consent, sender identification and a working unsubscribe are required. Spam Act 2003 summary, ACMA https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, checked 2026-11-02.
Enquiry and referral records hold personal information. Check the Privacy Act 1988 obligations before collecting new fields.

qualityStandard: A same-day first-reply target is set and tracked for each enquiry channel
Each referral request is specific and recorded with its source
No reactivation message is sent without a recorded consent basis
documentationEvidence: Enquiry process map with time targets
Referral and reactivation log with consent status and outcomes
summary: Fix the process before adding leads.
Ask for referrals at a milestone, with a specific request.
Reactivate only where consent is recorded; honour opt-outs at once.

knowledgeChecks.question: A process that loses enquiries is most likely fixed by:
options: Mapping and timing each step from first reply through to the initial visit
Buying more advertising, since more leads will fix a slow process
Lowering all prices across the menu, since cheaper work brings more clients

knowledgeChecks.question: When is a referral request best made?
options: During the first conversation with an enquirer today
After a client reaches a milestone and says they are pleased
In a mass message to strangers on a Friday afternoon

knowledgeChecks.question: Before sending an electronic reactivation message, the lesson requires:
options: The client's date of birth and street address, on the booking form
Consent that meets the Spam Act rules for that address

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that is free, works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. The page as read does not name the Spam Act 2003 and does not cover privacy law. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA).

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs and guidelines apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act; the page states that the Act covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some other organisations, without listing them. The page as read lists the APP chapters but does not set out collection or consent rules; the full text is in a linked PDF that was not read, so small business coverage and consent detail are UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC).
